title: Longest Valid Parentheses
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every substring directly versus a stack with a resettable base position that computes run length in one pass.

blocks.text: Given a string s containing just the characters '(' and ')', find the length of the LONGEST valid (well-formed) parentheses SUBSTRING (a contiguous run, not just any subsequence).

blocks.caption: A stack of indices, with a special "base" marker that resets whenever a close-parenthesis has nothing valid to match, tracks the current valid run's length directly

blocks.text: Unlike simply checking whether a whole string is validly matched, this problem needs the LENGTH of the longest contiguous SUBSTRING that is itself validly matched, which may be shorter than the whole string, and there could be multiple separate valid runs interspersed with invalid characters.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Longest Unbroken Streak of Correctly Paired Gloves
blocks.text: Imagine matching up gloves (left and right) laid out in a row, where correctly paired ones can chain together into a longer streak, but a mismatched or leftover glove breaks the streak entirely, starting a fresh count from right after it. This problem asks for the length of the LONGEST such unbroken streak anywhere in the row, not just whether the whole row is perfectly paired.

blocks.caption: When a close-bracket finds nothing to match (the stack becomes empty), it becomes a fresh "base" marking where the next potential valid run would begin

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The maximum run length observed is 4, matching the expected result

Before checking every possible substring for validity directly (expensive), notice that a stack of indices, combined with a "base" marker for wherever the current run last reset, directly tracks the current valid run's length as the string is scanned once.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: An opening bracket always gets pushed, remembering its position as a potential future match point.

Observation 2: A closing bracket first tries to pop (match) the most recently pushed position; if this SUCCEEDS (the stack still has something left afterward), the current valid run extends from just after whatever is now the new top all the way to the current position, a length directly computable via subtraction.

Observation 3: If popping empties the stack entirely, this closing bracket has NOTHING to match (an invalid, "broken streak" character); it becomes pushed itself, marking the new base position from which any future valid run would be measured.

Observation 4: Starting the stack with a sentinel value of -1 (representing "position just before the string begins") elegantly handles the very beginning of the string as if there were already a valid base there, avoiding special-case logic.

This is a stack-based technique tracking a "base" position: whenever a closing bracket successfully matches, the run length is computed directly as the current index minus whatever base is now exposed on top of the stack.
Check every possible substring (of even length, since odd-length substrings can never be validly balanced) for validity directly, tracking the longest one found.

items: For every starting index i and every even ending length, check whether that substring is a fully valid parentheses sequence (using a simple balance-counter check).
Track the maximum length among all valid substrings found.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Only even-length substrings are ever checked, since a valid parentheses sequence must have an equal number of opens and closes.
The validity check itself uses a simple running balance counter, going negative if a close ever exceeds the opens seen so far.

blocks.text: Correctly finds the longest valid substring, since every possible candidate substring is explicitly checked.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^3): O(n^2) substrings, each requiring an O(n) validity check.
Space: O(1) extra (excluding the substring being checked).
Limitation: checking every substring independently repeats a huge amount of overlapping work; a single stack-based pass with a "base" marker finds the answer directly in O(n).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force checks every substring from scratch. Instead, maintain a stack of indices, seeded with a -1 sentinel (representing the position just before the string starts). For each opening bracket, push its index. For each closing bracket, pop; if the stack becomes empty, push the current index as a new base; otherwise, the current valid run's length is the current index minus whatever is now exposed on top of the stack, updating the running maximum.

Initialize a stack with -1. Walk through s: for '(', push the index. For ')', pop; if the stack is now empty, push the current index (a new base); otherwise, compute i - stack.top() and update the maximum length seen so far.
Use a stack of indices with a -1 sentinel base, computing the current valid run's length directly whenever a closing bracket successfully matches.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The maximum length observed throughout is 4, matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single linear pass.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case.

The stack, at any point, holds exactly the "unmatched" positions: the -1 sentinel or the most recent base, followed by any currently-unmatched opening brackets. When a closing bracket successfully pops an opening bracket, whatever is now exposed on top of the stack is precisely the position just BEFORE the current valid run started, so subtracting it from the current index gives exactly that run's length. When a closing bracket has nothing to match (an invalid character), it correctly becomes the new "reset point" for measuring any future valid run.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["'(' encountered","Pushed, becoming a potential future match point"],["')' successfully matches (stack non-empty after popping)","Run length = current index - new stack top; update the maximum"],["')' has nothing to match (stack empties)","Push the current index as a new base for future runs"]]}

items: The initial -1 sentinel elegantly handles a valid run starting at index 0, since 0 - (-1) = 1 would correctly measure a length-1 (single character) scenario, and more generally sets up the base correctly from the very start.
Checking "stack is empty" immediately after popping (not before) correctly distinguishes a successful match from an unmatched closing bracket.
The running maximum is updated only on a SUCCESSFUL match, since an unmatched closing bracket cannot be part of any valid run.

blocks.text: Extending simple bracket-MATCHING (yes/no valid) to bracket-LENGTH (longest valid run) is achieved by tracking a "base" position on the stack, resetting it whenever a bracket has nothing to match, and computing the run length directly via index subtraction whenever a match succeeds.

items: Forgetting the initial -1 sentinel, which would require awkward special-casing for a valid run starting at the very beginning of the string.
Updating the maximum length even when a closing bracket fails to match (the stack becomes empty), incorrectly counting an invalid position as part of a valid run.
Confusing this with the simpler Valid Parentheses problem, which only needs a yes/no answer, not a length.

items: Explicitly explaining the ROLE of the -1 sentinel and why the stack top (after a successful pop) represents "the position just before the current run" clarifies the trickiest part of this technique.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "LONGEST valid parentheses SUBSTRING" (not just a yes/no validity check) points toward a stack tracking a resettable "base" position, enabling direct length computation on each successful match.

items: How would you solve this without a stack, using O(1) extra space instead? A two-pass approach (scanning left-to-right tracking open/close counts, then right-to-left) can achieve the same result without a stack, at the cost of a slightly less intuitive derivation.

How does this problem build on the simpler Valid Parentheses problem? It extends the SAME stack-based matching idea, additionally tracking a resettable base position specifically to measure the LENGTH of each successfully matched run.

What would change if the string could also contain other bracket types (e.g., [ and {)? The core "base" tracking idea would still apply, but the matching logic itself would need to verify TYPE correctness as well, similar to the original Valid Parentheses problem's type-checking.
A length-tracking extension of the core stack-based bracket matching technique from Valid Parentheses elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^3) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (stack with a base marker): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Stack-based bracket matching with a resettable "base" position

Core Idea: A stack of indices, seeded with -1, tracks the position just before the current valid run; a successful match computes the run's length directly via subtraction, while an unmatched close resets the base
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Whatever is exposed on the stack's top right after a successful pop is exactly the position just before the current valid run began
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Stack seeded with -1; pop on ')'; empty means new base, else length = i - new top
